Story: On Monday, 9 Elul 5674, Maharaitz set out for Lubavitch to attend to the affairs of Tomchei Temimim. He remained in the town until the afternoon of Wednesday 11 Elul, when he returned to the family's summer retreat at Zaalshe.
Tags: maharaitz, lubavitch, tomchei temimim, yeshiva

Title: Maharaitz's diary: outbreak of World War I observed at Zaalshe
Summary: Rebbe Yosef Yitzchak began a diary at the Zaalshe summer retreat covering the outbreak of the First World War.
Story: Beginning 13 Menachem Av 5674 (August 1914), while staying with his father at the Zaalshe summer retreat, Rebbe Yosef Yitzchak recorded daily entries about the outbreak of World War I. Maharashab followed the news closely through newspapers and visitors, expressed wonder at Germany's audacity to fight several nations at once, and refused to share his own opinions on the conflict.
Tags: maharaitz, maharashab, wwi, zaalshe, diary, germany

Title: Maharashab and Maharaitz travel from Zaalshe to Lubavitch
Summary: On 24 Menachem Av 5674, Maharaitz traveled to Lubavitch on Tomchei Temimim business and Maharashab joined him for the trip.
Story: On 24 Menachem Av 5674, Maharaitz set out from Zaalshe for Lubavitch to attend to yeshiva matters; Maharashab unexpectedly decided to accompany him. They arrived at 9:30 at night. Early the next morning Maharashab visited the great hall where the temimim slept and was deeply moved by their condition. He prayed for hours, visited the ohel of his ancestors, and returned to Zaalshe that afternoon, exhausted from the visit.
Tags: maharashab, maharaitz, lubavitch, tomchei temimim, yeshiva, ohel

Title: Maharashab speaks on yeshiva reform and balancing Torah with prayer
Summary: On 28 Menachem Av 5674, Maharashab discussed at length how the yeshiva must balance Talmudic study with avodah of prayer.
Story: On 28 Menachem Av 5674, Maharashab walked with his son and discussed the Tomchei Temimim yeshiva, including the dormitory conditions and the need for students to study Nigleh. He explained that although many bochurim who came to him wished to devote themselves more to prayer, he typically refused: both Torah and prayer were essential, and the leader needed wisdom to keep the matter pure of intent.
Tags: maharashab, tomchei temimim, yeshiva, education, chassidus, prayer

Title: Maharashab teaches Chassidus on Parshat Eikev
Summary: On Shabbat Parshat Eikev 5674, Maharashab delivered a maamar on 'V'haya Eikev Tishmaun' connected to the ongoing series.
Story: On Shabbat Parshat Eikev 5674, Maharashab delivered a discourse beginning 'V'haya Eikev Tishmaun' as part of an ongoing series explaining the union of Or (light) and Keilim (vessels) — that the connection occurs specifically in the inner aspect of the vessels.
Tags: maharashab, chassidus, maamar, parshat eikev

Title: Maharashab teaches Chassidus on Parshat Re'eh
Summary: On Friday before Parshat Re'eh 5674, Maharashab delivered a maamar continuing his series on the union of Or and Keilim.
Story: On the Friday of Parshat Re'eh 5674, Maharashab delivered a discourse beginning 'Re'eh Anochi Notein Lifneichem... et HaBrachah Asher Tishmeun' as part of his ongoing series on the union of light and vessels, including the exchange of their natures whereby the speaker draws downward and the vessel becomes elevated and attached.
Tags: maharashab, chassidus, maamar, parshat reeh

Title: Outbreak of World War I and Rebbe Rashab's prophecy of a long war
Summary: At the outbreak of WWI the Rebbe Rashab predicted a long, mutually destructive war and told chassidim to keep their businesses running.
Story: At the start of Elul 5674 several wealthy chassidim came to Zaalshe to ask the Rebbe Rashab's advice as World War I broke out. They assumed Russia would quickly be forced to seek peace against Germany and considered halting their business. The Rebbe told them to continue their commerce, saying the war would be long, in his words: "einer vet dem andern einshlingen un vet zikh mit im derverger" (one will swallow the other and choke on him together).
Tags: world war i, rebbe rashab, russia, germany, zaalshe, elul, prophecy

Title: Reports reach Lubavitch of German atrocities at Kalisz
Summary: Maharashab expressed astonishment at reports of the German massacre of civilians in conquered Kalisz.
Story: Newspapers and private reports brought news of German army conduct in conquered territory, especially in the city of Kalisz where civilians, women and children had been slaughtered. Maharashab marveled at this, suspecting initially that the reports might be war propaganda to inflame hatred, but added a teaching that kings face stricter judgment in the heavenly court because rulers stand higher in matters of providence.
Tags: maharashab, wwi, germany, kalisz, poland

Title: Outbreak of World War I on Tisha B'Av
Summary: World War I began on Tisha B'Av 5674, three weeks before Schusterman's birth.
Story: The First World War broke out on the ninth of Av 5674. Schusterman notes this in his memoir as a marker for his birth date, which came three weeks later in the town of Zlobin in White Russia.
Tags: world-war-i, russia, tisha-bav

Title: Birth of M. Schusterman in Zlobin
Summary: M. Schusterman was born on Friday, Erev Rosh Chodesh Elul 5674 in Zlobin to Eli son of Achiezer and Rachel daughter of Aharon Tzvi Hirsch.
Story: Schusterman was born in the town of Zlobin, situated between Homel, Bobruisk, Rogachov, and the Volhynian district. His mother related that there was a solar eclipse on the day of his birth. The birth came three weeks after the outbreak of World War I on Tisha B'Av.
Tags: zlobin, russia, birth, schusterman, solar-eclipse

Title: 17th wedding anniversary of Maharaitz and Rebbetzin Nechama Dina
Summary: 13 Elul 5674 marked Maharaitz's 17th wedding anniversary, with prayers for a son after three daughters.
Story: On 13 Elul 5674, the 17th anniversary of his own wedding, Maharaitz recorded a prayer for length of days, nachas from his three daughters, and a son who would be a yarei shamayim, a chassid, a great scholar, and successful in all his affairs. At the time he had only daughters; the diary entry reflects his deep yearning for a male heir.
Tags: maharaitz, nechama dina, anniversary, wedding

Title: 39th wedding anniversary of Maharashab and Rebbetzin Sterna Sarah
Summary: 12 Elul 5674 marked the 39th wedding anniversary of Maharashab and Rebbetzin Sterna Sarah.
Story: On 12 Elul 5674, the 39th anniversary of the wedding of Maharashab and Sterna Sarah, Rebbe Yosef Yitzchak recorded a heartfelt blessing in his diary that they should be granted length of days and years in pleasantness, true health, and great nachas from their children.
Tags: maharashab, sterna sarah, anniversary, wedding

Title: Jerusalem Beis Din publishes 'Emet UMishpat Kasuv' in favor of Kollel officials
Summary: On 16 Elul 5674 the Jerusalem Beis Din Tzedek published a public ruling supporting the Kollel Chabad officials against the gabbaim Bichowsky and Bagin.
Story: The ruling, titled 'Emet UMishpat Kasuv', came after the two gabbaim had returned abroad without completing the formal din torah. It formalized the beis din's position that the Jerusalem officials were vindicated. Even so, accusations and counter-accusations between the two camps continued in printed pamphlets for years afterward.
Tags: kollel chabad, beis din tzedek, jerusalem, bichowsky, bagin

Title: Rebbe Rashab begins Rosh Hashanah discourse on divine unity
Summary: On Rosh Hashanah 5675 the Rebbe Rashab opened a new chassidic discourse explaining 'one' from below upward and from above downward.
Story: At the start of 5675 the Rebbe Rashab began expounding the concept of divine unity in both directions during the Tishrei maamarim. When chozrim asked for elucidation he replied enigmatically that 'the ends and the edges do not yet come together.' Only mid-winter, in the course of further chazara, did he indicate that the matter had now been clarified.
Tags: rashab, maamar, lubavitch, rosh hashanah, chassidus, echad

Title: Tzarist conscription of yeshiva students intensifies
Summary: After Sukkot 5675 the Russian army began calling up successive age cohorts, including many yeshiva students.
Story: Following Sukkot 5675 the standard call-up of 21-year-olds was followed by ever-younger classes as the war intensified. Most Tomchei Tmimim students were drafted, and many of those discharged could not return to Lubavitch. The campaign reshaped the yeshiva's enrollment for the rest of the war.

Title: Wartime shortage of Calabrian etrogim in Lubavitch
Summary: Because of the war the Rebbe Rashab could not obtain Calabrian etrogim for Sukkot 5675, receiving only three from Eretz Yisrael.
Story: The outbreak of World War I cut off the usual supply of Calabrian etrogim. Three presumed non-grafted etrogim were brought from the Holy Land by R' Shneur Zalman Havlin, who had returned to Lubavitch that summer and was stranded by the war. The Rebbe Rashab was so distressed by the lack of Calabrian etrogim that he developed fever and facial swelling and did not attend shul on the first days of the festival.

Title: Birth of R. Abraham Kvash
Summary: R. Abraham Kvash was born on 1 Kislev 5675 in Kamenets-Podolsk, Ukraine.
Story: A future senior Tomchei Tmimim talmid, Kvash studied first in Kiev as a child before joining the underground Lubavitch yeshiva in Vitebsk in 1928. His biography becomes a thread in this chapter as the Rebbe Rayatz attempts to rescue him from Latvia where he would ultimately perish.

Title: Turkish government expels Russian-citizen Jews from Hebron
Summary: In Tevet 5675, the Ottoman government expelled Chabad Jews of Russian citizenship from the Land of Israel as nationals of an enemy power.
Story: R' Avraham Chaim Naeh recorded in the preface to his Shnos Chaim that the expulsion took place in Tevet 5675 (December 1914). Because much of the Chabad community in Hebron held Russian citizenship, they were forced out by Turkey as enemy nationals. Many of the exiles concentrated in Alexandria (No-Amon), Egypt.

Title: Rebbe Rashab recounts history on 19 Kislev
Summary: On 19 Kislev 5675 (6 December 1914), Rebbe Rashab told over the history of the Alter Rebbe's maamar-recording tradition.
Story: Speaking on the chag of redemption, Rebbe Rashab described how the Mitteler Rebbe's primary haNochos came from the post-Petersburg period rather than from Liozna. The transcript was preserved in Toras Shalom and provides a key source for the chronology of Chabad maamarim.

Title: 19 Kislev farbrengen 5675 in Lubavitch
Summary: On 19 Kislev 5675 the Rebbe Rashab held the Chag HaGeulah farbrengen in the large hall and spoke of events in the World of Truth.
Story: The annual 19 Kislev celebration in 5675 took place in the great hall at Lubavitch. The Rebbe Rashab discussed matters unfolding in the World of Truth; R' Moshe of Zembin asked 'what will become of us?' and the Rebbe responded that one should hold tight to his gartel. Wartime scarcity forced the gathering to make do with unfamiliar liquors, and the Rebbe ended the farbrengen when his wife came to ask that they cease searching for more.

Title: Death of R' Avraham Chaim, chassid in New York
Summary: R' Avraham Chaim, a senior chassid who emigrated to New York, passed away on the first day of Chanukah 5675.
Story: R' Avraham Chaim ben Dov Ber passed away on 25 Kislev 5675 (first night of Chanukah). He left a detailed will specifying no eulogies, no newspaper announcements, and burial directly touching the earth per the Zohar. Decades later in 5760, his grave was located not at the Achuzas Olam plot but at Mount Zion cemetery in Brooklyn, correcting an earlier transcription error that had given his death year as 5674.
Tags: chabad-america, avraham-chaim, new-york, burial

Title: Catalog of Rebbe Rashab's book collection compiled
Summary: A catalog listing 5,642 entries from the Rebbe Rashab's book collection was compiled.
Story: During 5675 (1915), a catalog was apparently prepared of the books in the Rebbe Rashab's library, listing 5,642 numbered entries representing approximately 12,000 volumes. The work began in early 5673 but the surviving list, which includes books printed up to 5670, was likely completed during 5675 since the books were placed in storage at the start of 5676. The catalog counted multi-volume sets like Shas as single entries.
Tags: library, lubavitch, catalog, bibliography

Title: Chafetz Chaim flees Radin to Russia with his yeshiva
Summary: In summer 5675, as Germany was about to conquer Radin, the Chafetz Chaim fled with a large portion of his yeshiva into Russia, beginning a six-year exile.
Story: He resided first in Smilavitchi, then Shumyatch, then Snovsk. He remained in Russia until summer 1921, when he returned to Radin. The Chafetz Chaim later wrote about being well-received and supported by communities in all three Russian locations.
Tags: chafetz chaim, radin, world war i, germany, yeshiva, smilavitchi

Title: Chafetz Chaim transfers yeshivah from Poland to Russia
Summary: Rabbi Yisrael Meir Kagan moved his Radin yeshivah from Poland to Russia at the beginning of World War I.
Story: The yeshivah remained in Russia until March 1921, when the elderly Chafetz Chaim returned it to Poland after expressing despair over the Communist regime and Jewish renegades. He later voiced regret over the departure.
Tags: chafetz-chaim, radin, ww1, poland

Title: Chatzkevich settles in Abel after WWI exile
Summary: Chatzkevich was forced from Ponimonek during the WWI expulsions and, upon return, was accepted as rabbi of the town of Abel.
Story: Chatzkevich remained in Ponimonek until the WWI-era expulsion of Jews from frontline regions. Upon returning from exile, he did not return to Ponimonek but instead was accepted as rabbi of the town of Abel.
Tags: chatzkevich, ponimonek, abel, wwi, exile

Title: Death of R' Moshe Rosenblatt of Zembin
Summary: R' Moshe Rosenblatt of Zembin, mashpia for younger students, passed away in Shevat 5675 in Lubavitch.
Story: R' Moshe Rosenblatt of Zembin was accepted at Tomchei Tmimim in 5669 as a mashpia for younger students. He served until his passing in Shevat 5675 (1915) in Lubavitch. He was known as 'Moshe der Chozer' for his role repeating the Rebbe Rashab's discourses at guest lodgings, and he typically opened each farbrengen with a niggun.
Tags: tomchei tmimim, lubavitch, rosenblatt, zembin, mashpia

Title: Frierdiker Rebbe leaves Lubavitch due to approaching war
Summary: In autumn 1915, due to the approaching enemy and the war, R. Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn left Lubavitch in the Mohilev district, storing his library of 35 wooden crates in the Kokorov warehouses in Moscow.
Story: The library, containing only religious books and prayer books in Hebrew, had been assembled over decades by his father and grandfather. The crates remained in those Moscow warehouses for years, becoming the subject of repeated requests for their return.

Title: Levitin sent to Georgia as chief shliach
Summary: Forced to leave Rakishok during WWI in 5675, Levitin was sent by the Rebbe Rashab to Georgia as chief shliach to establish a network of educational institutions.
Story: During World War I, in 5675 (1915), Levitin was forced to leave Rakishok. The Rebbe Rashab then sent him as chief shliach to Georgia, where he brought additional Tomchei Tmimim students and established a network of educational institutions, eventually building a major yeshiva in Kutaisi over roughly a decade.
Tags: levitin, georgia, kutaisi, rashab, yeshiva, wwi

Title: Library books transferred to storage in Moscow
Summary: The Lubavitch library's printed books were packed and sent to storage in Moscow during WWI.
Story: During Cheshvan 5676 (late 1915), all the printed books were packed into crates and sent for safekeeping, ultimately to Moscow rather than Nizhny as originally planned. The 5,430 numbered items (approximately 12,000 volumes) were placed in a secure storage facility protected against fire, water, and theft. The books were stored in the warehouses of the chassid R' Zalkind Persitz in the Kukurov district of Moscow.
Tags: library, moscow, wwi, books, persitz

Title: Lubavitch library packed and sent to storage in Moscow
Summary: When the Rashab evacuated Lubavitch at the start of 5676, the library's print collection was crated and sent to the Kokorev warehouses in Moscow for safekeeping.
Story: With the front of World War I advancing, the Rashab left Lubavitch carrying only his most-used books and the manuscript collection, sending the printed seforim to Moscow for storage. The crates were deposited at the warehouses of the wealthy chassid R. Zalkind Persitz. They would never return to family control: the warehouses were nationalized and the books transferred to state libraries, beginning the decades-long struggle to recover them.
Tags: library, rashab, lubavitch, moscow, wwi, kokorev-warehouses

Title: Maamar Shnei HaMeoros by Rabbi Yitzchak Aizik of Homil published
Summary: First edition of Maamar Shnei HaMeoros by Rabbi Yitzchak Aizik of Homil was printed in Poltava in 5675.
Story: This chassidic discourse by Rabbi Yitzchak Aizik of Homil was first printed in Poltava in 5675 (1915). It is one of several of his works in the Lubavitch Library's exhibition devoted to the great chassidim of Chabad.
Tags: poltava, yitzchak aizik homil

Title: Manuscripts taken to Rostov; library left in Moscow warehouse
Summary: When the Rashab fled to Rostov in 5676 he took the manuscripts of the Chabad Rebbes with him but left the large book collection in 35 crates in the Moscow warehouses of Zalkind Persitz.
Story: Thousands of books and hundreds of manuscript volumes were stored in Persitz's Moscow warehouses pending the family's intended return. The books were later seized and transferred to the Moscow public library, where they remain in exile to this day. The fate of these volumes would become a major decades-long campaign of the Chabad movement.

Title: R' Yosef Rosen, the Rogatchover Gaon, ends first Dvinsk tenure
Summary: R' Yosef Rosen of Rogatchov served as Dvinsk's Chassidic rabbi until 1915, when wartime conditions forced his departure.
Story: R' Yosef Rosen, the famed Rogatchover Gaon, served as Chassidic rabbi at the Planover Minyan inside Dvinsk until 1915 (5675). World War I forced him to leave the city, though he would return more than a decade later.

Title: R. Baruch Shalom Cohen returns to Russia during WWI
Summary: In the winter of 5675, during World War I, R. Baruch Shalom Cohen left the Warsaw region and resettled in Moscow.
Story: When the First World War swept through the Russian-Polish frontier in winter 5675 (1914-15), R. Baruch Shalom Cohen left Volomin and returned eastward into Russia, settling in Moscow. His departure marked the wartime disruption of the Volomin Tomchei Tmimim branch.

Title: Rashab delivers Simchat Torah warning about Kaiser Wilhelm
Summary: On Simchat Torah, the Rashab declared he knew Kaiser Wilhelm well from his European travels and could not dwell under his rule.
Story: The Rashab told the Chasidim: 'I know the kaiser well from the thirty years that I have been traveling outside Russia. He is an apikores (heretic), and under his rule I cannot dwell.' He recalled how during a public speech in Berlin, the kaiser had stared at them sharply and had police remove them, the Rashab interpreting it as Wilhelm already plotting war.

Title: Rashab flees Lubavitch in the face of German invasion
Summary: The fifth Rebbe, Rabbi Sholom Dovber (Rashab), fled the town of Lubavitch as the German army advanced during WWI.
Story: Chabad Rebbes traditionally wore the shtreimel only in Lubavitch. When the Rashab fled in the face of the German invasion in 1915, he ceased wearing it. The departure ended the historic Lubavitch chapter of Chabad, beginning years of wandering and persecution.

Title: Rashab speaks against Kaiser Wilhelm on Simchat Torah
Summary: On Simchat Torah, the Rashab denounced Kaiser Wilhelm as a heretic and refused to live under his rule.
Story: On Simchat Torah 1915, the Rashab declared, 'I know the kaiser well from the thirty years that I have been traveling outside Russia. He is an apikores, and under his rule I cannot dwell.' He recounted a Berlin episode in which Wilhelm had ordered police to remove him and the Rayatz from a public speech.

Title: Rebbe Rashab flees Lubavitch as German army advances
Summary: In the autumn of 5676 the Rashab and his family were forced to flee Lubavitch as the German army approached during World War One, eventually settling in Rostov-on-Don.
Story: After several weeks of travel they reached Rostov-on-Don, deep in the Russian interior far from the front. The Frierdiker Rebbe later recorded their hope to return to Lubavitch the following summer once the war ended. They never returned, and the departure proved to be the effective end of Lubavitch's century as Chabad's center.

Title: Rebbe Rashab flees Lubavitch for Rostov
Summary: Rebbe Rashab fled Lubavitch with his family during WWI and settled in Rostov, taking manuscripts and ~100 books while leaving most of his library in Moscow.
Story: At the start of 5676 (autumn 1915), as World War I disrupted Lubavitch, the Rashab moved his household to Rostov. He could not carry his entire library, so most books were stored in a Moscow warehouse (where they remained for decades). He brought along the manuscript collection and about one hundred books, including a Jerusalem Talmud printed in Zhitomir with his handwritten glosses.

Title: Rebbe Rashab forced to flee Lubavitch as German army approaches in WWI
Summary: At the start of 5676 (1915), as the German army approached Lubavitch, the Rebbe Rashab and his household were forced to leave the town, hoping to return after the war.
Story: World War I brought the front lines near Lubavitch, the longtime seat of Chabad. The Rebbe Rashab departed with his family, expecting the displacement to be temporary. In fact, this marked the end of Lubavitch's era as the center of the Chabad movement; the town's chassidic infrastructure would never be restored.

Title: Rebbe Rashab forced to flee Lubavitch due to WWI
Summary: The Rebbe Rashab and his family were forced to flee Lubavitch as the German army approached.
Story: At the start of 5676 (1915), during World War I, as the German army approached the Lubavitch area, the Rebbe Rashab and his household were forced to flee. The decision to leave Lubavitch was made during Tishrei 5676, with the primary concern being how to transport the book collection. The Rebbe took the manuscript collection with him to Rostov but stored the printed books elsewhere.

Title: Russian deportation of Jews from border provinces
Summary: As the World War I front advanced into Russia in 1915, the Russian government ordered Jewish residents to leave their towns within 24 hours, displacing them to interior provinces.
Story: During WWI, as the front line approached Jewish population centers in Russia, the government decreed that Jews must abandon their homes within 24 hours. This was carried out fully during the summers of 5675 and 5676, with Jews stripped of property and expelled from their towns. The refugees were assigned to five interior gubernias: Voronezh, Tambov, Penza, Crimea, and Yekaterinoslav. Although the decree was later rescinded, the Germans had by then captured the original Jewish areas, leaving the refugees stranded.

Title: Wife of R' Elchanan Dov Morozov dies in childbirth
Summary: The wife of R' Elchanan Dov Morozov died during childbirth in winter 5675 for lack of available physicians.
Story: In the winter of 5675 the wife of R' Elchanan Dov Morozov, sister of the noted tamim R' Avraham Dovid of Klimavichi, died in childbirth. The Rebbe Rashab attributed her death to the dictum 'there are those who perish without judgment,' since adequate medical care was unavailable in the small town at the moment of need.

Title: WWI expulsion order ends the Pale of Settlement in practice
Summary: A special order in 5675 required Jews to abandon any locality within 24 hours of the approaching front, effectively dismantling the Pale of Settlement.
Story: Most Pale provinces were declared front-zone areas in which Jewish residence was forbidden, and deportees were assigned to five interior provinces: Voronezh, Tambov, Penza, Crimea, and Yekaterinoslav. The decree was later rescinded, but by then German forces had occupied the original Jewish areas, leaving nowhere to return. The formal abolition came with the fall of the tsarist regime in 1917.

Title: Inheritance farbrengen for the Horowitz heirs in Lubavitch
Summary: In Shevat 5675 the heirs of the wealthy R' Yosef Yozik Horowitz held a farbrengen in Lubavitch after settling the inheritance.
Story: Sons, sons-in-law and a grandson of the late R' Yosef Yozik Horowitz, who had held a monopoly on button sales, came to Lubavitch to divide his estate before the Rebbe Rashab. Once arrangements were finalized they hosted a farbrengen on Thursday night at the home of R' Michael Katzenelnbogen, attended by mashpi'im, melamdim and select students. R' Moshe of Zembin and the Rashbatz debated the relative spiritual stature of the Rebbe Rashab, with R' Yitzchak Magidson defusing tension through niggun.
Tags: shevat, lubavitch, yosef yozik horowitz, moshe of zembin, samarkand gershon ber, farbrengen, yitzchak magidson

Title: Passing of R' Moshe of Zembin in Lubavitch
Summary: R' Moshe of Zembin passed away in Binyamin's Shtibel in Lubavitch on the Friday after the inheritance farbrengen in Shevat 5675.
Story: On the morning after the all-night Horowitz farbrengen, R' Moshe of Zembin went to the mikveh and felt unwell. He was brought into the nearby Binyamin's Shtibel, where R' Dovber Shmotkin obtained medicine from Yehoshua's pharmacy that briefly revived him. He died there before Shabbos; the Rebbe Rashab cancelled the planned chassidus and asked whether any further attempts at resuscitation could be made, and the levaya was held on Motzaei Shabbos.

Title: R' Alter Simchowitz marries Rivka Havlin in Lubavitch
Summary: In Shevat 5675 R' Alter Simchowitz married Rivka, daughter of the mashpia R' Shlomo Zalman Havlin, in Lubavitch.
Story: Havlin was the director of Yeshivat Toras Emet in Hebron and later in Jerusalem. The marriage cemented a tie between two influential Chabad educational figures of the era.
Tags: lubavitch, alter simchowitz, shlomo zalman havlin, marriage

Title: Twenty-year-olds called up for Russian military service
Summary: In January 1915 the Russian army summoned men born twenty years earlier to military service.
Story: As the war ground on, Russia expanded conscription downward through the age groups. January 1915 brought the call-up of twenty-year-olds, many of them yeshiva students at Tomchei Tmimim. The yeshiva ranks thinned dramatically as the draft progressed.

Title: Purim 5675 farbrengen at the Rebbe Rashab's home
Summary: The Rebbe Rashab held a Purim 5675 farbrengen in his dining room, said chassidus, and davened maariv after midnight.
Story: Purim 5675 began with a small gathering at the Rebbe's table where he discussed knowledge and free will, including whether gentiles possess true bechirah. As the night progressed the entire chassidic community joined and the Rebbe delivered a maamar. Maariv was davened at roughly 1:45 a.m., the latest the author had ever witnessed.

Title: Nineteen-year-olds drafted; author called to register
Summary: In May 1915 men born in 1896 were summoned for army service; the author registered and received a one-year deferment.
Story: By May 1915 the Russian military extended the draft to nineteen-year-olds belonging to the 1916 conscription class. The author traveled home, presented himself, received a one-year exemption, and returned to Lubavitch for the summer. The conscription pattern foreshadowed yet younger cohorts being called later that year.

Title: Secret farbrengen with R' Shlomo Zalman Havlin before draft
Summary: Students arranged a clandestine farbrengen with R' Shlomo Zalman Havlin before fellow student Shmuel Kadish Bertanovsky departed for the draft.
Story: When Shmuel Kadish Bertanovsky had to leave Tomchei Tmimim to present himself for conscription, the author and a few others arranged a covert gathering. Government liquor shops were shut by wartime decree, so Moshe Gurary paid two roubles for a single bottle of kummel. R' Havlin spoke of how Chabad chassidus brings the soul's innermost essence into revealed expression through the intellect and emotions, and the farbrengen lasted from late Thursday night until six in the morning.

Title: Eighteen-year-olds drafted into the Russian army
Summary: In August 1915 the Russian army called up eighteen-year-olds belonging to the 1917 class.
Story: The widening draft reached the eighteen-year-old cohort by August 1915, followed soon after by the 1918 class. The cumulative effect emptied much of Tomchei Tmimim of its students. The yeshiva struggled to retain a viable learning population.
Tags: world war i, russia, draft

Title: R. Elchanan Yakubovitz appointed second rabbi of Lubavitch
Summary: On 23 Av 5675 the householders of Lubavitch appointed wartime refugee R. Elchanan Yakubovitz as a second rabbi alongside R. Dovid Yakobson.
Story: When R. Elchanan b. Avraham Shimon Yakubovitz, former rosh mesivta of Telz, fled to Lubavitch during World War I, the householders of the town's two main shuls appointed him as a second rabbi on 23 Menachem Av 5675 (August 1915). The forty signatories agreed to a monthly salary of thirty rubles and authorized him to rule on routine questions in the Shliove and Lachluka street synagogues. The Rashab approved, and Yakubovitz also taught in the Tomchei Tmimim yeshiva.
Tags: elchanan yakubovitz, lubavitch, rabbinate, wwi, refugee

Title: Maharashab and family leave Lubavitch for Rostov
Summary: On Sunday 16 Cheshvan 5676, Maharashab departed Lubavitch with his entire household amid the upheavals of World War I.
Story: On Sunday, 16 Cheshvan 5676 (October 1915), Maharashab left Lubavitch together with his entire family. Earlier accounts based on Chanoch L'Naar and the Rebbe Rayatz's letters had suggested they reached Rostov around mid-Kislev, but the dated passport stamps reveal a much shorter journey of less than two weeks.
Tags: maharashab, lubavitch, rostov, wwi, exile, evacuation

Title: Rashab evacuates Lubavitch as the war front approaches
Summary: In Marcheshvan 5676 the Rashab and his household evacuated Lubavitch ahead of the advancing front line.
Story: As World War I drew nearer to Lubavitch, the Rashab departed the town with his family in Marcheshvan 5676 (October/November 1915), ending the 102-year period in which Lubavitch served as the worldwide capital of Chabad. The newly installed second rabbi R. Elchanan Yakubovitz also left at this time, his tenure as Lubavitch's rabbi having lasted only a few months.
Tags: rashab, lubavitch, wwi, evacuation, rostov

Title: Rebbe Rashab denounces Kaiser Wilhelm at Simchas Torah farbrengen
Summary: On Simchas Torah 5676 the Rebbe Rashab spoke harshly of Germany and Kaiser Wilhelm, calling them Amalek.
Story: At the pre-hakafos farbrengen in his home on Simchas Torah 5676 the Rebbe Rashab spoke at length about Germany and Kaiser Wilhelm. He declared that he had known the Kaiser for thirty-one years, that he was Amalek whose end is destruction, and contrasted the Germans as 'apikorsim Amalekim' with the French and Africans. The farbrengen ran through the night and the hakafos that evening were not held.
Tags: simchas torah, rashab, germany, kaiser wilhelm, amalek, world war i, lubavitch

Title: Rebbe Rashab letter on plans to send books to Nizhny
Summary: The Rebbe Rashab wrote of plans to send the library books to Nizhny for safekeeping.
Story: On 27 Tishrei 5676 (October 5, 1915), the Rebbe Rashab wrote to R' Shmuel Michel Trainin that he might travel from Lubavitch within a few weeks with his entire household. He planned to send the books, which were numerous, for safekeeping and could not delay until the last moment. His initial plan was to send them to Nizhny, though they ultimately went to Moscow.
Tags: war, wwi, library, relocation, books

Title: Council in Lubavitch over whether to leave the war zone
Summary: Family and close chassidim convene in Lubavitch for a five-hour deliberation on whether and where the Rebbe Rashab should evacuate.
Story: On 10 Marcheshvan 5676, R. Shmuel Michel Trainin and R. Shmuel Gourary arrived from Petrograd and met in the Rebbe Rashab's room with him, the Rebbetzin Shterna Sarah, and the Rayatz. They debated whether to remain in Lubavitch, move to a major city, or travel to the Caucasus health resorts. After about five hours it was resolved that the whole family would travel together, though the destination was still undecided.
Tags: lubavitch, world war i, rebbe rashab, rayatz, shmuel michel trainin, shmuel gourary

Title: Rebbe Rashab visits the graves of his ancestors before departing Lubavitch
Summary: Before leaving Lubavitch, the Rebbe Rashab spends about four hours at the gravesites of his Chabad predecessors.
Story: On Thursday, 13 Marcheshvan 5676, the Rebbe Rashab traveled to the resting places of the previous Chabad Rebbes in Lubavitch. He remained there for roughly four hours and returned with eyes red from weeping, traces of which were still visible the following day. That night he told the Rayatz of his hope that the German army would not reach Lubavitch.
Tags: lubavitch, ohel, rebbe rashab

Title: Last maamar of Hemshech Tarav: Shabbos Vayera 5676 "Cholas Ahava"
Summary: The Rebbe Rashab delivered the closing maamar of Hemshech Tarav on Shabbos Vayera 5676, the day before leaving Lubavitch.
Story: On Shabbos Parshas Vayera 5676 the Rebbe Rashab delivered the maamar on the inyan of "cholas ahava," the final maamar of the Hemshech that had begun on Shavuos Tarav. The next day, Sunday Parshas Chayei Sara, the Rebbe and his entire household relocated from Lubavitch.
Tags: vayera, rebbe rashab, hemshech tarav, cholas ahava, lubavitch, maamar

Title: Maharashab arrives in Rostov-on-Don
Summary: Maharashab and his family arrived in Rostov-on-Don on Friday 28 Cheshvan 5676, establishing the new Chabad headquarters there.
Story: On Friday 28 Cheshvan 5676 (23 October 1915), Maharashab's passport was stamped in Rostov-on-Don, documenting the precise date the Rebbe and his household reached their new home in exile. The discovery of this passport stamp corrected earlier estimates and confirmed the family's testimony that the journey from Lubavitch to Rostov took less than two weeks.
Tags: maharashab, rostov, wwi, exile, lubavitch

Title: Rashab abandons Lubavitch and relocates family to Rostov-on-Don
Summary: The Rashab, his son, and their families departed Lubavitch on 16 Cheshvan, fleeing the advancing German army.
Story: After 102 years as home to four Chabad Rebbes, the sun set on Lubavitch. The historic Chabad library was packed into thirty-five crates and placed in storage in Moscow, while the Rashab took valuable manuscripts with him. The Rashab told the Chasidim 'We hope to return... before Passover' but they never returned. They settled in Rostov-on-Don, 700 miles south of Moscow.

Title: Rashab departs Lubavitch for Rostov-on-Don
Summary: On 16 Cheshvan, the Rashab and his family abandoned Lubavitch ahead of the German advance, relocating to Rostov-on-Don.
Story: On 16 Cheshvan 5676 (October 24, 1915), after 102 years of four Chabad Rebbes calling Lubavitch home, the Rashab and his family departed for Rostov-on-Don, seven hundred miles south of Moscow. The library was packed into 35 crates and stored in Moscow; the Rashab brought the valuable manuscripts with him.
Tags: lubavitch, rostov, rashab, wwi, library, relocation

Title: Rebbe Rashab and family leave Lubavitch for Rostov
Summary: On Sunday, 16 Marcheshvan 5676, the Rebbe Rashab departed Lubavitch with his entire household.
Story: At 11 a.m. on Sunday, 16 Marcheshvan 5676 (24 October 1915), Rabbi Sholom DovBer Schneersohn left Lubavitch with his family, intending to return the following summer. He took the Rebbeim's manuscripts and a limited selection of books, while the bulk of the library — thousands of volumes in 35 crates — was deposited with the chassid R' Zalkind Persitz in Moscow. The hoped-for return never came, and a year-after-year exile began.
Tags: rashab, lubavitch, rostov, russia, world war i, exile

Title: Rebbe Rashab and family leave Lubavitch for the south
Summary: On Sunday 16 Cheshvan 5676 the Rebbe Rashab and his family departed Lubavitch for safer territory deeper in Russia.
Story: With the German army nearing Belarussia and Russian authorities seizing Jewish leaders as hostages near the front, the Rashab was forced to leave Lubavitch. Preparations had begun after Sukkot with wooden crates built for the seforim, and on Parshat Vayera he delivered a discourse on the levels of cholat ahavah. On 16 Cheshvan he departed; he stopped in the city of Ariel for several weeks before settling in Rostov-on-Don in the Cossack region.
Tags: lubavitch, rashab, exile, world war i, russia, rostov, ariel

Title: Rebbe Rashab leaves Lubavitch for the last time
Summary: The Rebbe Rashab, his family, and 97 puds of luggage depart Lubavitch by train, never to return.
Story: On Sunday, 16 Marcheshvan 5676, at 11:00 a.m., the Rebbe Rashab left Lubavitch as the German advance pressed eastward. Students of Tomchei Temimim, the staff, the town rav, townspeople, and even non-Jewish neighbors gathered in the courtyard to take leave of him. The stationmaster at Rudnya personally supervised the loading of the family's 97 puds of luggage onto the train.
Tags: lubavitch, world war i, rebbe rashab, tomchei temimim, exile

Title: Rebbe Rashab relocates from Lubavitch with his family
Summary: The Rebbe Rashab left the town of Lubavitch with his entire family the day after Shabbos Vayera 5676.
Story: On Sunday Parshas Chayei Sara 5676, the day after delivering the closing maamar of his great Hemshech, the Rebbe Rashab departed Lubavitch with his entire family. The town of Lubavitch had been the Rebbes' seat since the Mitteler Rebbe; the departure marked the end of the Lubavitch era as the front lines of WWI advanced.
Tags: rebbe rashab, lubavitch, chayei sara, world war i, relocation, russia

Title: Rashab departs Lubavitch ahead of German advance
Summary: Rabbi Shalom Dovber and his family departed Lubavitch on October 25, 1915, ending its century as Chabad's capital.
Story: On October 25, 1915 (17 Cheshvan 5676), the Rashab and his family departed Lubavitch in the face of the advancing German army during World War I. With his departure, Lubavitch's 102-year run as the capital of the Chabad chasidic movement came to an end. The Rashab never returned to Lubavitch, though the yeshivah remained in the town for another two years.
Tags: lubavitch, russia, world war i, german invasion, rashab

Title: Rebbe Rashab arrives in Orel
Summary: After about 29 hours on a crowded train, the Rebbe Rashab reaches Orel and is hosted by R. David Fradkin.
Story: On Monday evening, 17 Marcheshvan 5676, the Rebbe Rashab's party arrived in Orel at 7:00 p.m. after a tightly packed journey of roughly twenty-nine hours. Unable to find suitable lodgings, they stayed in three rooms at the home of R. David Fradkin while sharing a common dining room. Despite efforts by R. Yaakov the shochet, no permanent residence in Orel could be secured.
Tags: orel, russia, rebbe rashab, david fradkin, world war i

Title: Rebbe Rashab leaves Orel for Rostov-on-Don
Summary: After eight days in Orel, the Rebbe Rashab boards an express train direct to Rostov-on-Don.
Story: On Tuesday, 25 Marcheshvan 5676, the Rebbe Rashab left Orel after eight days of cramped lodging. With R. David Fradkin's help, tickets were obtained on the express train running straight to Rostov-on-Don, and the family's luggage traveled with them. Fradkin himself accompanied them to see them off.
Tags: orel, rostov, russia, rebbe rashab, world war i

Title: Rebbe Rashab arrives in Rostov-on-Don
Summary: After a stopover in Orel, the Rashab reached Rostov on Wednesday morning, 26 Marcheshvan 5676.
Story: Leaving Lubavitch on 16 Marcheshvan, the Rashab's party traveled some 29 hours to Orel, remained there until 25 Marcheshvan, then took the express train and arrived in Rostov at 10 a.m. on Wednesday, 26 Marcheshvan 5676. His internal Russian passport was stamped two days later, on 23 October 1915 (Julian) — 28 Marcheshvan. Rostov would remain the seat of Chabad leadership for the rest of his life.
Tags: rashab, rostov, russia, world war i, exile

Title: Rashab moves into rented Rostov apartment on Pushkinsky Street
Summary: On Friday, 5 Kislev 5676, the Rashab's household entered their first rented apartment in Rostov.
Story: After two weeks in a hotel and a difficult search for housing, the Rashab moved his family into an apartment on Pushkinsky Street on erev Shabbos, 5 Kislev 5676. He described the rooms as good and high-ceilinged on a wide street, but complained in a Chanukah letter that the landlord was unpleasant and spoke improperly. The 19 Kislev farbrengen that year was held in this new apartment.
Tags: rashab, rostov, pushkinsky

Title: Rebbe Rashab moves into apartment on Pushkinskaya Street, Rostov
Summary: After nine days at the Hotel Petrograd, the Rebbe Rashab settles into a six-room rented flat at 166 Pushkinskaya Street.
Story: On Friday, 5 Kislev 5676, the Rebbe Rashab moved his household into a rented apartment at 166 Pushkinskaya Street in Rostov. The previous tenant had only vacated at 2:00 p.m., furniture had not yet arrived, and the electric wiring was unfinished, yet the Rebbe insisted on moving in before Shabbat. A telephone (number 19-89) was installed in the following days as the family adjusted to urban Rostov life.
Tags: rostov, russia, rebbe rashab, pushkinskaya

Title: First Yud-Tes Kislev farbrengen in Rostov
Summary: Chassidim converge on Rostov for the Rebbe Rashab's first Yud-Tes Kislev in the city, where he delivers the maamar 'Padah Beshalom.'
Story: On 19 Kislev 5676 (Friday), chassidim arrived in waves at the Rebbe Rashab's new home in Rostov, with delegations from Kharkov, Homel, Minsk, Kremenchug, and elsewhere. On Thursday evening the Rebbe delivered the maamar 'Padah Beshalom Nafshi' lasting over an hour, and on Friday evening, despite displeasure that so many had come during wartime, he said the maamar 'Karov Havayah Lechol Korav.' The Shabbat meal continued for two hours of Torah and inspiration, and a closing Sunday meal stretched until 7:00 p.m.
Tags: rostov, yud tes kislev, rebbe rashab, maamar, chassidim, farbrengen

Title: R' Mordechai Dovber Slonim, head of Kollel Chabad Hebron, passes away
Summary: R' Mordechai Dovber Slonim, the appointed head of Kollel Chabad in Hebron, died on 5 Tevet 5676 amid the wartime collapse of the community.
Story: While the chief rabbi Shila and the yeshiva director R' Shlomo Zalman Havlin had fled to Russia at the start of the war, R' Mordechai Dovber Slonim remained behind in Hebron. Unable to withstand the suffering of the war years, he passed away in good name on 5 Tevet 5676. With his death, only a remnant of Chabad's Hebron leadership survived.
Tags: hebron, kollel chabad, slonim, wwi

Title: Partial rabbinic exemption granted by Russian government
Summary: The Russian government agreed to exempt or extend exemption deferments for fifty rabbis on the lists, a small fraction of those awaiting decisions.
Story: After persistent lobbying, the government granted exemption or extended deferments for approximately fifty rabbis on the conscription lists. This represented only a small fraction of those awaiting decisions, and it remained unclear whether the exemption came by direct Imperial decree or only by ministerial decision. The Rebbe Rashab immediately wrote to Reb Shmuel Michel Trainin to clarify the details and try to bring the matter before the Tsar.
Tags: russia, world war i, conscription, rabbis, exemption

Title: Rabbis face conscription crisis over registration deadlines
Summary: During summer 5676, rabbis who had missed initial conscription appearances faced refusal of their exemption status from military officials.
Story: As the summer of 5676 progressed, the conscription appearance date arrived for rabbis. Most rabbis assumed they were not required to report, since provincial governors had already been instructed to submit lists of practicing rabbis. Military officials in Yekaterinoslav and apparently Minsk concurred, issuing exemption certificates pending clarification. However, other officials ruled that rabbis who failed to appear at the original call-up had forfeited their exemption. The Rebbe Rashab enlisted the prominent Petrograd lawyer Oskar Gruzenberg, who learned from Deputy Interior Minister Baltz that such rabbis would face trial for non-appearance but retained their underlying exemption rights.
Tags: russia, world war i, conscription, rabbis, oskar gruzenberg, yekaterinoslav, minsk

Title: Rashab and family flee Lubavitch for Rostov
Summary: As the German army approached during WWI, Rashab and his family fled Lubavitch and settled in Rostov-on-Don in early 5676.
Story: At the start of 5676 (late 1915), with World War I raging and the German army advancing toward the Lubavitch region, Rashab and his household were forced to flee Lubavitch. After spending several days in Orel, they settled in Rostov-on-Don, deep within the Russian interior. The Tomchei Tmimim yeshiva also relocated.
Tags: rashab, rostov, lubavitch, wwi, evacuation

Title: Rayatz arrested in St. Petersburg
Summary: The Rayatz was again imprisoned in St. Petersburg for advocating military exemptions for young Jewish men.
Story: In 1916, the Rayatz was arrested for the fourth time between 1911 and 1916, again connected to his efforts to exempt young Jewish men from military service. As before, the detention was brief and ended with a warning rather than charges.
Tags: rayatz, arrest, st petersburg, military exemptions

Title: Rayatz imprisoned again in St. Petersburg over military exemption
Summary: The Rayatz was imprisoned in St. Petersburg again because of his efforts to exempt young men from Russian military service.
Story: This was his fourth arrest. The Rayatz's far-reaching public activities and watchful defense of Russian Jewry's rights aroused the displeasure of the czarist regime. Government inquiries found nothing incriminating and he was released with a stern warning, only spurring him to greater efforts.
Tags: rayatz, st petersburg, arrest, military exemption

Title: Rebbe Rashab campaigns for rabbinic exemption from conscription
Summary: In summer 5676 the Rebbe Rashab began intensive efforts to obtain government exemption from military conscription for rabbis, shochtim, cantors and other religious functionaries.
Story: In March 1916 (Adar Sheni 5676), the Russian Interior Minister sent a circular to provincial governors ordering police to identify serving rabbis and forward the lists for conscription review. Recognizing the catastrophe that would befall Jewish religious life if rabbis and shochtim were drafted, especially during wartime displacement, the Rebbe Rashab traveled to Petrograd to consult with local rabbis and activists. A memorandum was prepared for the Interior and War Ministers; though Mr. Markon delayed signing it through Pesach, Baron Alexander Gunzburg and lawyer Sliozberg eventually submitted their own memorandum on rabbinic exemption to the Interior Minister.
Tags: russia, world war i, conscription, rabbis, shochtim, petrograd, tsarist russia

Title: Rebbe Rashab dispatches rabbis to Soviet Georgia
Summary: Responding to a request from community leaders in Kutaisi, the Rashab sent Shmuel Levitin and other rabbis to establish a yeshivah for Sephardic Jews.
Story: The Georgian community was steeped in tradition but lacked rabbis and scholars. The Rashab sent Levitin, Slavin, Sasonkin, Perlow, and Zuber, among others. Decades later, when the underground emissary Simon Yakovshvili returned to Georgia, the region's Jewish life remained vibrant enough to alarm Yevesektzia leader Moshe Litvakov.
Tags: kutaisi, georgia, sephardic, shmuel-levitin

Title: Russian decree on conscription of displaced rabbis
Summary: A second Russian government circular extended conscription registration requirements to displaced rabbis from border towns, complicating their exemption process.
Story: While the initial conscription circular addressed only resident rabbis, a follow-up order extended the registration requirements to rabbis who had been displaced in summer 5675 from the border districts. These cases had to be processed through officials at the rabbis' original places of residence, from which they had been deported, severely impeding orderly clarification. Throughout summer 5676, the Rebbe Rashab continued to advocate for their status.
Tags: russia, world war i, refugees, conscription, displaced rabbis

Title: Scarlet fever epidemic strikes Lubavitch
Summary: A scarlet fever epidemic struck children in Lubavitch in winter 5676, killing a yeshiva student and others.
Story: During the winter of 5676 scarlet fever spread through Lubavitch and children died daily, a calamity locals linked to the homemade liquor production prompted by the government ban. The town rav, R' David Yaakovson, declared a ban on the illicit distilling. One yeshiva student from Homel named Aharon died; his fellow students sat with him around the clock and buried him in Lubavitch.
Tags: lubavitch, scarlet fever, askera, epidemic, world war i, homemade liquor, david yaakovson

Title: Rebbe Rashab delivers maamar on yahrtzeit of Rebbetzin Rivkah in Rostov
Summary: On the yahrtzeit of his mother Rebbetzin Rivkah, the Rebbe Rashab delivers the maamar 'Vayehi Beshalach Pharaoh' in Rostov.
Story: On Shabbat 10 Shevat 5676, parshat Beshalach, the Rebbe Rashab marked the yahrtzeit of his mother, the Rebbetzin Rivkah. He delivered the maamar beginning 'Vayehi Beshalach Pharaoh,' a brief notation of which appears in the Rayatz's short daily diary for that year.
Tags: rostov, rebbe rashab, rebbetzin rivkah, yahrtzeit, maamar, parshat beshalach

Title: Rayatz begins composing his account of the move to Rostov
Summary: In Rostov the Rayatz begins writing his detailed reshimah recounting the family's evacuation from Lubavitch via Orel.
Story: Starting on 2 Adar I 5676 in Rostov, the Rayatz set down a meticulous record of the decision to leave Lubavitch, the journey, the first reception in Rostov, the apartment search, the inaugural Yud-Tes Kislev farbrengen in the new home, and the troubles with the landlord. The composition continued through Purim Katan of that same year.
Tags: rostov, rayatz, reshimot, memoir

Title: Rebbe Rashab's Purim Katan maamar in Rostov
Summary: Over Shabbat Purim Katan in Rostov the Rebbe Rashab delivers the maamar 'Ve'ahavta et Havayah.'
Story: For Shabbat Purim Katan 5676 Rabbi Y.Y. of Kremenchug came to Rostov, and R. Tzvi Gurary, who had planned to leave Thursday night, stayed on to spend Shabbat with the Rebbe Rashab. The Rebbe delivered the maamar 'Ve'ahavta et Havayah Elokecha,' which was preserved in a separate written record.
Tags: rostov, purim katan, rebbe rashab, maamar, kremenchug

Title: R' Yaakov Landau dispatched as covert envoy to refugee towns
Summary: The Rebbe Rashab secretly sent Rabbi Yaakov Landau of Kornitz to assess the spiritual conditions of displaced Jews in Russia's interior.
Story: The Rebbe Rashab dispatched Reb Yaakov Landau of Kornitz (later rabbi of Bnei Brak) as a covert emissary to survey the religious state of the Jewish refugees. Landau departed shortly after Purim 5676 for a month-long journey and was forbidden to reveal his mission to anyone. He returned about a week before Pesach and delivered his report to the Rebbe on the night of bedikat chametz at Rostov, having returned for Shabbat HaGadol as the Rebbe had commanded.
Tags: russia, world war i, refugees, r' yaakov landau, kornitz, reconnaissance

Title: Rebbe Rashab founds religious aid committee in Petrograd
Summary: In late winter 5676, after a rabbinic assembly in Petrograd, the Rebbe Rashab founded a religious committee to provide for the spiritual needs of WWI Jewish refugees.
Story: The interior gubernias to which refugees had been displaced were outside the former Pale of Settlement and lacked synagogues, chadarim, mikvaot, and other religious institutions. The Rebbe Rashab traveled to Petrograd immediately after Purim 5676 to address this, organizing a special committee through an assembly of rabbis and activists. The committee, headed by Reb Shmuel Michel Trainin, worked to establish chadarim and Talmud Torahs, mikvaot, and to supply tefillin, tzitzit, and siddurim in the refugee locations.
Tags: russia, petrograd, world war i, refugees, chadarim, mikvaot, r' shmuel michel trainin

Title: Maharashab travels from Rostov to Petersburg
Summary: Maharashab's passport was stamped in Petersburg on 18 Adar II 5676.
Story: On 10 March 1916 (18 Adar II 5676), several months after settling in Rostov, Maharashab traveled to Petersburg, with his internal passport stamped accordingly.
Tags: maharashab, petersburg, rostov, passport, wwi

Title: Maharashab travels to Petersburg
Summary: Maharashab's passport was stamped in Petersburg on 7 Iyar 5676.
Story: On 27 April 1916 (7 Iyar 5676), Maharashab returned to Petersburg, marking his second wartime visit to the Russian capital from Rostov.
Tags: maharashab, petersburg, passport, wwi

Title: Rebbe Rashab travels to Petrograd to finalize rabbi exemption
Summary: On 4 Iyar 5676 the Rebbe Rashab traveled (or prepared to travel) again to Petrograd to finalize lobbying for rabbinic and shochet exemption from military service.
Story: On the 4th of Iyar 5676, the first day of Parshat Behar, the Rebbe Rashab prepared to journey again to Petrograd. The purpose was to bring to completion the lobbying efforts with government ministers to exempt rabbis and shochtim from military service. He returned home for the festival of Shavuot.
Tags: russia, petrograd, world war i, conscription, rabbinic exemption

Title: Rebbe Rashab begins effort to exempt rabbis from Russian army service
Summary: The Rebbe Rashab launched a sustained campaign during summer 1916 to secure military draft exemptions for Russian rabbis and shochtim.
Story: From Sivan 5676 (mid-1916) through Tevet 5677, the Rebbe Rashab worked from Rostov to coordinate efforts through his agents in Petrograd — primarily R. Sh. M. Trainin, later joined by R. Eliezer Ginzburg of Moscow — to obtain draft exemptions for rabbis and ritual slaughterers (shochtim). Letters were written to government ministers, and attorney Oscar (Israel) Grosenberg was engaged. The effort was complicated by distinctions between holders of blue and white identity cards.
Tags: russia, tsarist, wwi, military exemption, rabbinate, trainin, grosenberg

Title: Maharashab visits the mineral baths at Slavyansk
Summary: Maharashab traveled to the mineral baths at Slavyansk on 14 Sivan 5676.
Story: On 2 June 1916 (14 Sivan 5676), Maharashab traveled to the Slavyansk mineral baths, continuing the family tradition of seeking healing waters that his father had begun at Marienbad decades earlier.
Tags: maharashab, slavyansk, mineral baths, health, wwi

Title: Petition over young rabbis' exemption status
Summary: On 19 Tammuz 5676 the Rebbe Rashab protested to Reb Shmuel Michel Trainin that young rabbis under age 25 had been removed from the exemption list.
Story: Reb Shmuel Michel Trainin reported through Reb Shmuel Gourary that the Director of the Religious Department had removed rabbis under age 25 from the exemption list. The Rebbe Rashab wrote that he could not understand why these rabbis should be excluded, since they had been certified by local police as serving rabbis. He argued that those who attained the rank of horaah at young ages were especially elevated, having dedicated all their days to Torah, and should not be excluded.
Tags: russia, world war i, conscription, young rabbis, r' shmuel michel trainin

Title: Rebbe Rashab requests consultation meeting in Petrograd
Summary: On 18 Tammuz 5676 the Rebbe wrote to R. Sh. M. Trainin urging an organizational meeting to advance the rabbis' exemption.
Story: In letter 1056 the Rebbe Rashab stressed that without a face-to-face gathering of activists, nothing would move forward. He asked the committee to decide whom to invite, when, and where, and to send invitation letters.
Tags: russia, petrograd, trainin, letter

Title: Author arrested as draft evader in Chernigov
Summary: In mid-Elul 5676 the author was jailed in Chernigov as a deserter after presenting irregular papers during a mobilization.
Story: On the Rebbe Rashab's advice the author traveled to Chernigov to seek help from the Rabbi Dovid Tzvi Chen rather than register as a rabbi near Zhuravichi. A surprise mobilization led the local police to demand his documents, which were not in order, and he was held with army deserters for four days. Through the intervention of communal leader R' Mordechai Polai he was released on Shabbos afternoon and brought before a fresh medical board which granted him a white discharge ticket.
Tags: chernigov, draft, world war i, russia, rebbe rashab, rebbe of chernigov, david tzvi chen, arrest

Title: Russian government certification of Lubavitch rabbinic appointment
Summary: On 2 September 1916 Russian authorities formally certified R. Dovid Yakobson's confirmation of the 1915 rabbinical appointment letter.
Story: More than a year after the original 23 Av 5675 Hebrew rabbinical appointment letter for R. Elchanan Yakubovitz was drafted, the document received Russian civil certification on 2 September 1916. The Lubavitch starosta endorsed it with his seal alongside R. Dovid Yakobson's signature attesting that the 40 Hebrew signatures were genuine. The delay points to the dislocations of the wartime evacuation period.
Tags: lubavitch, elchanan yakubovitz, dovid yakobson, russia, civil registration

Title: R. Eliezer Ginzburg of Moscow joins exemption effort
Summary: On 20 Elul 5676 the Rebbe Rashab formally pulled R. Eliezer (Leib) Ginzburg of Moscow into the Petrograd rabbinical committee work.
Story: The Rebbe wrote to Trainin asking that Ginzburg be summoned to Petrograd. Ginzburg eventually traveled there after Yom Kippur and made multiple trips, including a planned visit to Rostov to consult with the Rebbe in person.
Tags: moscow, petrograd, ginzburg, rabbinical committee

Title: Maharashab returns to Rostov
Summary: Maharashab's passport was stamped on his return to Rostov on 14 Tishrei 5677.
Story: On 28 September 1916 (14 Tishrei 5677), just before Sukkot, Maharashab's internal passport was stamped in Rostov, recording his return to the family's wartime base.
Tags: maharashab, rostov, passport, wwi

Title: Rosh Hashana 5677 with the Rebbe Rashab in Slavyansk
Summary: The author and many Tomchei Tmimim students traveled to the Rebbe Rashab in the seaside resort town of Slavyansk for Rosh Hashana 5677, defying an order from the Rayatz that students not come.
Story: The Rebbe Rashab had summered in Slavyansk in 1916 and remained there through Rosh Hashana. The Rayatz, then yeshiva director, had instructed that no student travel for the chag, but nearly all the older bochurim came anyway. The students lodged in vacated summer cottages and subsisted largely on stale black bread and tea, while important guests were hosted at the Rebbe's table. A newly built local mikveh cracked overnight, forcing the Rebbe to walk to the town mikveh on Rosh Hashana morning.
Tags: rosh hashana, slavyansk, tomchei tmimim, rashab, russia, wwi

Title: Sukkot 5677 at the Rebbe Rashab's court in Rostov
Summary: After Rosh Hashana the students traveled from Slavyansk to Rostov for Sukkot 5677, despite a directive against it; Calabrian etrogim were scarce and they lodged with the Gertzulin family alongside Novardok mussar students.
Story: The Tomchei Tmimim students received return tickets after Rosh Hashana but were warned not to go on to Rostov; the author and several others went anyway. Calabrian etrogim, the chassidic standard, were in short supply because of the war. The students were hosted by the family of Mordechai Gertzulin and his mother Chana, where they also encountered Novardok mussar students for the first time and debated their approach to prayer. Lacking means to set up a sukkah at their first lodging, they built one at a Rostov house used by Tomchei Tmimim students from that city.
Tags: sukkot, rostov, tomchei tmimim, etrog, novardok, russia, wwi

Title: Simchat Torah farbrengen with the Rebbe Rashab in Rostov
Summary: On Simchat Torah 5677, under wartime restrictions, seven Tomchei Tmimim students who had stayed behind to review the Rebbe Rashab's maamar were warmly received at his clandestine farbrengen and unusually invited to say l'chaim.
Story: Wartime conditions had been declared: no public gathering was to take place at the Rebbe's home, and infractions risked being shot on sight. After the hakafot the gabbai R' Elchanan Dov Morozov quietly announced that everyone should go home and that there would be no farbrengen. Seven bochurim — including the author, R' Yisrael Feigin, and Zalman Dovid Michelin — stayed behind to chazer the maamar. When they later climbed to the upper floor, they found the Rebbe Rashab seated with chassidim; he had a table brought for them, waited for each to wash and make hamotzi, and invited each one to say l'chaim — an honor previously unheard of for students.
Tags: simchat torah, rostov, farbrengen, maamar, rashab, wwi, russia

Title: Author leaves Chernigov for new Tomchei Tmimim branch in Kherson
Summary: Around 19 Kislev 5677 the author received word from the Rebbe Rashab, via R' Shmuel Zalman Havlin, to relocate from Chernigov to a newly founded Tomchei Tmimim branch in Kherson.
Story: While studying under the Rad'tz, R' Dovid Tzvi Chen, in Chernigov, the author received instructions just before 19 Kislev 5677 directing him and four classmates to join a new Tomchei Tmimim branch opening in Kherson. The discipline among the talmidim was such that no one questioned the move — the author packed up immediately. R' Tzvi Gottlieb of Kovno served as rosh mesivta in Kherson; there was no mashpia yet. Local supporters, including R' Yisrael Tchertok and the Bezpalov brothers (sons of the rav of Poltava), housed and fed the students generously.
Tags: kherson, tomchei tmimim, 19 kislev, chernigov, rad'tz chen, russia

Title: Arabic-script Haggadah translated by Hillel Farchi printed in Egypt
Summary: Hillel Farchi published a Sephardic-custom Haggadah with an Arabic translation in Arabic script in Egypt.
Story: In 5677 (1917), Hillel Farchi produced a Haggadah following Sephardic customs accompanied by an Arabic translation rendered in Arabic letters. Printed by Reuven Muskovitch in Egypt, the 42-page edition aimed to make the Seder accessible to Egyptian Jews more familiar with Arabic script than with Hebrew transliteration. The work reflected the linguistic realities of early 20th-century Egyptian Jewry.
Tags: haggadah, arabic, egypt, sephardic, hillel farchi

Title: Author returns to Chernigov to seek draft exemption
Summary: At the end of summer 5677 the author returned to Chernigov when Russia recalled even fully exempt 'white-ticket' men to the army, traveling to Nezhin to consult R' Menachem Mendel Chen about his father's status as a shochet.
Story: As the war ground on, the Russian government broadened conscription to include men previously released with white tickets. The author's father, fearing he would be called up despite serving as a shochet, sent his son to Nezhin to consult R' Menachem Mendel Chen, son of the Rad'tz, who had connections that might secure an exemption. The author spent a day there and was deeply impressed when the rav sat down at eleven at night to learn a sugya from mishna through Tosfos, explaining each word as if teaching a small child. The author was ultimately exempted again 'through the upper channels.'
Tags: chernigov, nezhin, wwi, draft, rabbi mendel chen, shochet

Title: Bolshevik Revolution
Summary: The Bolshevik revolution in Russia ushered in subdued religious life in Lubavitch and across the country.
Story: In 1917, the Bolshevik revolution transformed Russia, bringing Communist rule that would dramatically constrain Jewish religious life. After the revolution, religious life in Lubavitch continued in a subdued fashion under increasing pressure from Soviet authorities. The revolution set the stage for decades of suppression of Chabad and other Jewish religious activities.
Tags: russia, soviet union, bolshevik revolution, communism

Title: Chofetz Chaim's yeshiva relocates to Shumyachi during the revolution
Summary: Between 1917 and 1920, as Jews from Latvia, Lithuania and Poland were resettled into Belarus and Ukraine, the Chofetz Chaim and his yeshiva ended up in Shumyachi, where the author's future father-in-law R' Zusman Fradkin became close to him.
Story: The upheavals of the Russian Revolution displaced great Torah institutions along with their host communities. R' Zusman Fradkin, the Shumyachi shochet and acting rav, drew close to the Chofetz Chaim during this period and received from him, even though R' Zusman himself had learned in Slobodka and was a Chabad chassid by inclination. R' Zusman was murdered with his sons by the Nazis on 29 Adar 5702.
Tags: chofetz-chaim, shumyachi, radin, displacement, fradkin, russian-revolution

Title: Father drafted to World War I army
Summary: Levin's father Ephraim Shmuel was conscripted into the army in the middle of World War I, leaving the mother to support the family.
Story: During the height of World War I, Ephraim Shmuel was taken to the front, forcing Leah Beila to run their small shop and continue the children's education on her own. She was unusually learned for a woman of her region, having attended cheder herself, and taught the children Hebrew reading, Tanach, grammar, and arithmetic. Ephraim Shmuel returned home in 1918 and reopened his cheder.
Tags: world war i, russia, draft, zhivotov

Title: First Bais Yaakov school founded by Sarah Schenirer in Poland
Summary: Sarah Schenirer founds the first Bais Yaakov, pioneering formal Torah study for Orthodox women.
Story: The Schenirer schools focused on basic Jewish literacy, traditions, and history but did not emphasize chasidic theology. The Rebbe's later Achot Hatemimim initiative would go further, promoting serious study of Tanya and chasidic discourses.
Tags: bais-yaakov, schenirer, poland, women

Title: R. Shmaryahu Mekler elected Vitebsk delegate to the Moscow conference
Summary: The Vitebsk philanthropist R. Shmaryahu Mekler was chosen in 5677 as the city's representative to the rabbinical conference held in Moscow.
Story: In 5677, in the upheavals surrounding the Russian Revolution, the Vitebsk askan and gevir R. Shmaryahu Mekler was elected as the city's delegate to the rabbinical conference held in Moscow. He had earlier been among the lay leaders who backed the 1910 cheder-teachers' petition to the St. Petersburg conference, and his role in 1917 marks the continuity of anash communal organizing into the revolutionary period.
Tags: russia, vitebsk, moscow, shmaryahu-mekler, russian-revolution

Title: Rad'tz Chen quietly dissolves Chernigov Jewish party assembly
Summary: When a public Chernigov assembly meant to elect delegates for a religious Jewish party (likely Netzach Yisrael) drifted from observant aims, R' Dovid Tzvi Chen quietly maneuvered to dissolve it.
Story: Under the Provisional Government, plans were underway for a national Jewish assembly in Kharkov to elect a council overseeing religious and educational affairs, and parties of every stripe were sending emissaries to local towns. A visiting rabbi came to Chernigov on behalf of a religious party — the author recalls it being called Netzach Yisrael or similar — and the Rad'tz himself attended the public meeting. Sensing during the speeches that the gathering did not in fact reflect truly observant priorities, the famously otherworldly Rad'tz acted with quiet practical wisdom and dissolved the assembly, and no delegates were chosen for that faction.
Tags: chernigov, jewish politics, netzach yisrael, kerensky, rad'tz chen

Title: Rayatz at Moscow and Kharkiv assemblies
Summary: The Rayatz took a leading part in assemblies of rabbis and laymen in Moscow and Kharkiv.
Story: In 1917 and 1918, against the backdrop of revolution and civil war, the Rayatz played a prominent role in rabbinic and lay assemblies convened in Moscow and Kharkiv to grapple with the future of Russian Jewish communal life.
Tags: moscow, kharkiv, rayatz, assemblies, rabbinic leadership

Title: Rayatz takes leading part in rabbinic assemblies in Moscow and Kharkiv
Summary: The Rayatz took a leading role in major assemblies of rabbis and laymen convened in Moscow and Kharkiv.
Story: These assemblies addressed urgent communal concerns during the chaotic period of revolution. The Rayatz participated again in 1918. By this time he had spent over two decades involved in essentially every major concern facing Russian Jewry as his father's secretary and emissary.
Tags: rayatz, moscow, kharkiv, rabbinic assembly

Title: Rebbe Rashab issues general letter to Chassidim
Summary: The Rebbe Rashab printed a general letter to chassidim in 1917, on the eve of revolutionary upheaval in Russia.
Story: The 5677 (1917) general letter was issued by the fifth Chabad rebbe during a turbulent year that included Russian revolution and the relocation of his court. Printed exemplars are preserved in the library exhibition.
Tags: rebbe rashab, michtav kelali, russia

Title: Rebbe Rashab's public letter in Iyar 5677
Summary: In Iyar 5677, during the Kerensky era in Russia, the Rebbe Rashab published a general letter.
Story: In Iyar 5677 (May 1917), during the brief Kerensky government in revolutionary Russia, Rabbi Sholom Dovber Schneersohn (the Rebbe Rashab) issued a general public letter, later printed in his Igros Kodesh, vol. II, no. 469. The letter addressed his Chassidim during a turbulent period preceding the Bolshevik takeover.
Tags: russia, kerensky, public letter

Title: Russian Revolution
Summary: Czar Nicholas II abdicated and was later executed amid the Russian Revolution.
Story: In 1917, after years of anti-Jewish policy and wartime turmoil, Czar Nicholas II abdicated, ending the Romanov dynasty. He was later executed. The October Bolshevik Revolution that followed ushered in the Communist era and a new chapter of persecution for Russian Jewry.
Tags: russia, revolution, nicholas ii, bolsheviks

Title: Russian Revolution ends czarist regime; Nicholas II abdicates
Summary: Czar Nicholas II abdicated and was executed, ending the Russian czarist regime, and the Pale of Settlement decree was terminated.
Story: The revolution brought enormous upheaval. The Pale of Settlement, originally established by Catherine the Great in 1791, was terminated. Following the Communist Revolution, Jews were granted freedom to live anywhere in Russia. The Bolshevik Revolution and subsequent civil war led to Communist consolidation of power, alarming the Rashab and his family.
Tags: russia, revolution, nicholas ii, pale of settlement, bolsheviks

Title: Russian Revolution ends restriction on Jewish presses
Summary: The condition where only two Hebrew printing houses operated in all of Russia, imposed in 5597, continued until the 1917 Russian Revolution.
Story: The Rebbe Rayatz noted that the Tzarist limitation of only two Jewish presses in Russia — in Vilna and Zhitomir — persisted from the 5597 decree until the 1917 revolution. This 80-year bottleneck was a major reason chasidic publishing remained sparse through the eras of the Maharash and Rashab. After the revolution Hebrew publishing in Russia briefly opened up before new Soviet restrictions emerged.
Tags: russia, revolution, censorship, hebrew printing

Title: Summer 5677 fire devastates Lubavitch
Summary: A fire swept through Lubavitch in the summer of 1917, destroying the author's quarters along with his seforim and writings and two cabinets of seforim belonging to R' Elchanan Dov Morozov in an adjacent house.
Story: The alarm bell rang while the author was at the mikveh together with R' Avraham Dovid Poizner of Klimovich. They misjudged the direction of the fire and ran first to Poizner's home to rescue his Vilna Shas, hauling the seforim to dry ground at the riverbed. When the author reached his own lodgings at the home of R' Michael Katzenelenbogen, the roof was already alight; his brother Shlomo Tzvi was guarding their bedding. Several bochurim had tried to salvage furnishings but most was lost, including the author's books and writings and two large cabinets of seforim belonging to R' Elchanan Dov Morozov in the neighboring house.
Tags: lubavitch, fire, tomchei tmimim, seforim, morozov

Title: Yevesektzia founded as Jewish section of the Communist Party
Summary: Established to consolidate Bolshevik control over the Jewish masses, the Yevesektzia became the Rebbe's primary adversary.
Story: Many of its members came from the secular Bundist workers' party, which was historically hostile to Jewish religious observance and Zionism. Led by Semyon Dimenstein, the Yevesektzia frequently exceeded Soviet policy in attacking synagogues, schools, and religious leaders.
Tags: yevesektzia, communist-party, dimenstein, bund

Title: Maharashab travels to Petersburg
Summary: Maharashab's passport was stamped in Petersburg on 29 Tevet 5677.
Story: On 10 January 1917 (29 Tevet 5677), just weeks before the February Revolution, Maharashab visited Petersburg, his passport receiving another stamp at the capital.
Tags: maharashab, petersburg, passport, wwi

Title: Rebbe Rashab travels to Petrograd during February Revolution
Summary: In Shevat 5677 the Rebbe Rashab traveled to Petrograd and remained there through Purim, during which the February Revolution toppled the Tsarist regime.
Story: Having promised in mid-Tevet to travel within two weeks, the Rebbe arrived in Petrograd in Shevat and stayed until after Purim. During this period the February Revolution broke out, the Tsarist regime fell, and the democratic Provisional Government was established. No letters of his from Shevat-Adar 5677 survived.
Tags: russia, petrograd, february revolution, tsar, provisional government

Title: February Revolution topples Tsar Nikolai II
Summary: At the end of winter 5677, while the author was learning in Kherson, the Russian Revolution removed Tsar Nikolai II and the Provisional Government took power.
Story: The Rebbe Rashab responded with three open letters: one congratulating the Provisional Government, one urging chassidim to purchase shares in the new state loan, and one calling on chassidim and observant Jews to organize for upcoming communal elections now that Jews enjoyed full civil rights. He quipped that 'our God-fearing brothers excel at sluggishness.' Religious and Torah-aligned political parties began forming across Russia in response.
Tags: russian revolution, tsar, provisional government, russia, rashab, civil rights

Title: Author returns to Lubavitch and revives Kupat Bachurim
Summary: After Pesach 5677 the author returned to Lubavitch with his brother Shlomo Tzvi and, finding the yeshiva impoverished by war and revolution, refounded the Kupat Bachurim society to support hungry students.
Story: Train service had broken down, so the author traveled via Mohilev by steamboat to Orsha and onward by wagon. He found Lubavitch sharply diminished — the Rav's home in ruins, R' Zalman Fradkin visibly hungry when he came to the bochurim's dining hall, students rationed roughly two litras of bread per day. Shabbos challot were now baked small and of plain wheat flour. The author convened the older talmidim and refounded the Kupat Bachurim mutual aid society, writing to married Tomchei Tmimim alumni in scattered towns for help and securing supplemental support for the neediest students.
Tags: lubavitch, tomchei tmimim, kupat bachurim, famine, wwi, mohilev

Title: Mother of Shmuel Kadish Bartnovsky dies before Pesach
Summary: Before Pesach 5677 the mother of the author's classmate Shmuel Kadish Bartnovsky passed away; the author accompanied him as far as Nikolaev before returning to Kherson and home for the chag.
Story: While the author was studying in the Kherson yeshiva, his close friend Shmuel Kadish Bartnovsky lost his mother in the weeks leading up to Pesach 5677. The author traveled with him to Nikolaev to accompany him in his grief, then returned to Kherson and made his way home for Pesach. He returned to Lubavitch after the chag with his younger brother Shlomo Tzvi, who was to study there.
Tags: bartnovsky, kherson, nikolaev, pesach

Title: R' Alter Simchowitz appointed mashgiach in Shchedrin
Summary: On 16 Iyar 5677, the Rebbe Rashab arranged for R' Alter Simchowitz to be sent to Shchedrin as mashgiach.
Story: On 16 Iyar 5677 (1917), the Rebbe Rashab wrote that R' Alter Simchowitz, who had come from Eretz Yisrael, should travel via Lubavitch to receive instructions from R' Shilem and from the office, before continuing to Shchedrin as mashgiach for chassidut. Simchowitz, son-in-law of R' Zalman Havlin, stayed in Shchedrin until 5679 when the yeshiva closed and moved to Kremenchug.
Tags: tomchei tmimim, shchedrin, simchowitz, mashgiach

Title: Rebbe Rashab inquires about rabbis' exemption under Provisional Government
Summary: On 22 Iyar 5677 the Rebbe wrote to Trainin expressing concern about renewed debate over rabbis' military status under the new democratic regime.
Story: After the Provisional Government took power in winter 5677, discussion reopened on church-state separation and rabbinic conscription. The Rebbe wrote that he had long feared the question would resurface and was surprised no one had updated him from Petrograd.
Tags: russia, provisional government, separation of religion and state, trainin

Title: Rabbis assembly convenes in Moscow
Summary: At the close of Av 5677 a rabbis' assembly met in Moscow and resolved to elect a committee preparing the All-Jewish Congress.
Story: The assembly chose a committee to organize voting for Jewish community councils that would in turn elect the All-Jewish General Congress. It was decided the committee would sit in Petrograd alongside the general elections commission; the committee later relocated to Kharkov when Petrograd proved impractical.
Tags: moscow, rabbinical assembly, jewish congress

Title: Rebbe Rashab convenes Moscow rabbinic assembly
Summary: After the February 1917 Russian Revolution, the Rebbe Rashab worked to organize a religious united front, culminating in a Moscow rabbinic assembly in early Elul.
Story: Following the collapse of the Tsarist regime and establishment of the Provisional Government in the winter of 5677, elections were planned for Jewish community councils and a general Jewish Congress to organize Jewish communal life. The Rebbe Rashab fought to organize a religious front against anti-religious factions. He pushed for an assembly of Torah giants in Russia, which Rabbi Chaim Ozer wanted to instead achieve through founding Agudas Yisrael branches. The assembly was ultimately convened in early Elul in Moscow, where the proposal to found a permanent rabbinical association was rejected by the participants.
Tags: russia, moscow, russian revolution, provisional government, jewish congress, agudas yisrael, rabbi chaim ozer, rabbi eliezer rabinowitz
